newsitem.title: UK: Sickly rand pins hopes on foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: Sickly rand pins hopes on foreign investment.

text.p: The South African rand, which lost nearly a third of its value last year, needs a return of foreign investment before a sustained recovery can take place, London-based analysts said.
The rand's slide, which began in February last year, was exaggerated by a range of concerns including worries over the health of President Nelson Mandela and worsening economic fundamentals.
But the driving force behind the fall was a haemorrhaging of domestic capital overseas amid speculation about the impact of a relaxation of foreign exchange controls on the currency.
Rather than a reversal of that flow, analysts now see an increase in foreign capital flows into South Africa as the key to the rand sustaining a comeback.

"Long-term we definitely need to see an improvement in reserves, a sustained improvement in capital inflow and capital investment coming into the country," said Mitul Kotecha, treasury economist at Standard and Chartered here.
The rand dropped 31 percent between February and November to 4.7670 per dollar. It has since recovered to 4.4350.

Although the rand is highly unlikely to get back to levels seen before the drop, economists said an improvement in domestic fundamentals are already enticing foreign capital to the country and bodes well for further recovery of the currency.
"Sentiment has definitely improved since the start of the year," said Kotecha at Standard Chartered. "General fundamentals should improve over the year to yield a more bullish outlook."
Investors hungry for yield are currently eyeing bumper short-term yields at 16 percent.
An expected halving of the current account deficit to less than five billion rand in 1997 from just over 10 billion last year has also helped stabilise the currency so far in 1997.
The rand's value has historically been influenced by the current account deficit and when a broker's circular last February pointed to a worsening trade situation, the rand fell.
"The rand has typically had a good correlation with the external position and the increased focus on that fact has helped the rand," said Paul Lambert, senior currency economist at UBS here.

Economic growth is forecast to pick up at the end of this year and rise by 2.9 percent in 1998 while the consumer price inflation is set to fall throughout this year to 7.5 percent year-on-year by the fourth quarter.

Although an easing of exchange controls in South Africa might look a dangerous backdrop for some investors holding rand, analysts said a lot is already priced in and further relaxation is unlikley to see investors head for the exit in a big way.
"We're expecting that (relaxation of exchange controls) to happen in a piecemeal fashion and it's also been priced in to some extent," UBS's Lambert.
Investors have also taken some faith from the prudent approach of reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals who has been running policy to promote economic stability, analysts said.
However, there are still concerns about the political scene in South Africa.
"I can't see politicians facing elections in the near future having the same set of priorities," said Richard Gray, emerging markets economist at BankAmerica. "They must achieve growth."
South Africa is due to hold its next general election in April 1999.

Gray at BankAmerica said South Africa's huge unemployment rate, which some estimate to be as high as 40 percent of the adult population, would force the country's politicians to press for some acceleration of economic growth.
Threatening inflation rules out a relaxation of monetary policy, and a budget deficit at six precent of gross domestic product leaves little room for a relaxation of fiscal policy.
An easy way for South Africa to generate growth would be to let the rand fall further, boosting export competitiveness and thereby close the current account gap.

But analysts argue that the current account shortfall could also be offset by an inward flow of investment. "If Stals' calculation that capital flows do carry on increasing is guaranteed, then it's arguable that the foreign capital flows will dig them out of the hole," said BankAmerica's Gray. --London Forex Desk +44 171 542 6284
